advisor_letter:
David,

Most retirement reports treat the corporation as a side asset bolted onto a personal plan. Yours doesn't work that way. The retained earnings inside your CCPC are not just savings — they're the structural centerpiece of how income, taxes, and timing fit together over the next 15 to 30 years. Any plan that ignores that hierarchy gets the order of decisions wrong.

Ten years out from your target retirement, the question isn't whether the math works. It does. The real question is the sequence: how much income to extract from the corporation versus draw on the registered side; when to trigger the business sale at age 65; and how the layering of corporate dividends, RRSP/TFSA withdrawals, and CPP/OAS produces a tax-efficient retirement income.

This report walks through the trajectory, the income mix, and the leverage points specifically with the CCPC structure in mind. The order of the analysis follows the order in which the decisions matter — not a generic checklist.

For any specific decision arising from this analysis, please consult a certified financial planner familiar with your full situation.
overall_assessment: The plan is excellent at **100 %**. The structural strength is the corporation: **480K$** in retained earnings layered with **$250K** annual revenue acts as a parallel retirement vehicle alongside the **345K$** personal savings — that combined capacity is what produces the durability. The single zone deserving attention is the order of extraction in retirement: the corporate income, the RRSP/TFSA balances, and CPP/OAS each have different tax treatments, and the sequence in which they're drawn over the **40-year horizon** determines lifetime tax outcomes more than any single rate.
verdict: The dispersion is unusually narrow — the percentile bands collapse at the same value (**209K$**) — because your income capacity (corporate plus personal) is large enough relative to spending that market variance has limited impact on the retirement outcome. This kind of compression suggests the plan's robustness comes from structural redundancy, not from any single asset or assumption.
page_zero_verdict: You've built two engines (the corporation and the personal portfolio), and you want to know they'll run in tune through retirement — without one cannibalizing the other.
profile_summary: Personal savings total **345K$**: **180K$** RRSP, **95K$** TFSA, **70K$** non-registered. The corporation holds **480K$** in retained earnings on **$250K** of annual revenue, with a planned business sale at age 65. The **66.7 % equity / 33.3 % bond** allocation is appropriate for a 10-year accumulation horizon. The corporation is the centerpiece; the personal accounts are the diversifying complement.
trajectory_insight: The percentile bands compress at **209K$** at end of horizon — the corporate income capacity dominates the personal savings trajectory, so market variance shows up less in the wealth path. Savings durability is reported as never depleted across the simulated range. The plan would benefit from explicit mapping of how retained earnings convert to retirement income post-sale.
income_insight: Government coverage sits at **27 %** of retirement spending: CPP at **$1,687/month** plus OAS at **$1,421/month** total **$3,107/month** against a target of **$7,500/month**. The remaining **$8,245/month** gap is filled from the personal portfolio and corporate dividends. The corporation's role as an income engine becomes the dominant lever once the salary stream ends.
taxInsight: The lifetime effective tax rate is **16.4 %** with no projected OAS clawback — both reflect the income-smoothing benefit of having the corporation as a separate tax entity. The optimized strategy already captures **186K$** in lifetime tax alpha versus a naive baseline. The dominant lever is the salary/dividend mix during the remaining accumulation years, which sets the integrated rate for both the corporation and you personally.
estateInsight: Projected net estate of **357K$** after **117K$** in tax at death — primarily on the RRSP/RRIF balance. The corporation's residual value at death adds another layer that's not captured in the personal estate number; if the company is wound down at sale (age 65), the estate question simplifies considerably.
corp_insight: Retained earnings at **480K$** function as a tax-deferred parallel to the RRSP, with the integrated rate determining whether income should flow as salary (RRSP room, CPP credits) or be retained for later dividend extraction. The planned sale at 65 brings the lifetime capital gains exemption into play — coordinating that event with the RRSP-to-RRIF conversion at 71 is the structural decision that compounds across the next 30 years. Consult a tax-qualified planner for the integration math.
riskInsight: The narrow P25–P75 band reflects an income capacity well-matched to spending — the dispersion is dominated by tax-treatment uncertainty (rules change over 40 years) rather than market variance. The structural risk to monitor is concentration: the corporation accounts for a meaningful share of household wealth, so the post-sale diversification plan matters.
stress_interpretation: All six stress scenarios land at **100 %** success — gfc2008, stagflation73, longevityPlus5, lostDecade, persistentInf, and even spendingUp15 — because the corporate income engine plus the personal savings produce more capacity than any single shock can absorb. The compression confirms that the plan's robustness is structural, not market-dependent. Consult a certified financial planner for any decision stemming from this analysis.
